Now I'm looking at the regulatory context for Cumberland County — it's in the Ozone Transport Region, which means stricter NOx thresholds apply for major sources in nonattainment areas. The county falls under the Philadelphia-Wilmington marginal to moderate ozone nonattainment classification, and in the OTR, VOC and NOx are treated as if the area were in moderate nonattainment, which affects the 100 tpy threshold.

steps.title: Reasoning
steps.why:
Looking at the Philadelphia-Atlantic City ozone nonattainment area, this is classified as serious, which means the major source threshold for NOx drops to 50 tons per year. The facility's NOx emissions of 5,887 tpy far exceed that threshold, making it a major source requiring New Source Review with a 1.2:1 offset ratio — meaning I'd need to secure roughly 7,064 tons per year of NOx emission reduction credits, which is practically impossible to find in New Jersey. PSD regulations also apply to this situation.

The location itself is deeply problematic from an environmental justice perspective: it's in downtown Vineland, just 343 meters from a school and 177 meters from a hospital, with 476 points of interest within a kilometer radius. This is clearly an overburdened community. I notice the gas pipeline distance wasn't returned in the data, and while the API indicated 68 fields were available, only about 40 appear in the visible results — demographics, terrain, and land cover values are missing from what I can see.

I'm going to call determine_pathway next and batch in requests for the missing Class I area distance (Brigantine Wilderness is a Class I area in New Jersey that's likely within 100 kilometers) and the gas pipeline information.

facts.value: The nearest interstate natural gas transmission pipeline to 39.4862, -75.0257 is 34,019 meters (approximately 34 km) away, operated by Columbia Gas Trans Co, per the HIFLD Gas Transmission Pipelines dataset. The EIA's 10 km proximity buffer returned null — confirming no interstate pipeline exists within that tighter radius — but the unbounded HIFLD query resolved a real distance at ~34 km. Diameter, line pressure, and firm transport capacity are not geospatial attributes and were not returned by the dataset; these must be confirmed directly with Columbia Gas Trans Co as part of any tap feasibility assessment. For a 400 MW gas-fired plant, a 34 km lateral to the nearest interstate trunkline represents a material infrastructure gap requiring operator-confirmed capacity, tap lead time, and lateral construction cost before fuel supply can be assumed viable.

steps.title: Reasoning
steps.why:
Looking at the major nonattainment NSR pathway with a 41-104 month timeline and announced energization in 16 months — this is essentially dead on arrival. The Class I field request failed and needs a location example to retry, while the nearest gas pipeline is 34 kilometers away through Columbia Gas Trans, making that lateral a significant constraint. For step 7, I'm testing config changes to see what could work since synthetic minor is infeasible at 67 hours per year — SCR combined with dry low NOx technology might be viable.

Testing three configurations: SCR plus dry low NOx on a simple cycle, combined cycle with SCR and dry low NOx, and fuel cell. The SCR reduces NOx by 90%+ but even dropping from 5,887 to 300-500 tpy keeps us over the 50 tpy major nonattainment NSR threshold. A combined cycle improves heat rate but still lands around 350 tpy with SCR. Realistically, only a fuel cell approach gets a 400 MW gas plant under 50 tpy NOx in a serious ozone nonattainment area. The site itself fails the major nonattainment NSR test, which is the explicit trigger, though crossing into Delaware or Pennsylvania across the bay or state lines doesn't help since the whole OTR is nonattainment. I'll batch test these configurations — I've used 8 calls so far and have room to explore.

steps.title: Reasoning
steps.why:
Looking at the emissions control scenarios, SCR with DLN cuts NOx to 182.5 tpy and dramatically reduces offsets from 7,064 down to 219 tons—a major practical win even though it stays classified as a major NNSR source. The combined cycle with SCR achieves lower emissions at 111 tpy NOx and triggers the 28-source list due to crossing the 100 tpy PSD threshold, though it still qualifies as major NNSR since that threshold is 50 tpy. The fuel cell option appears to be the minimum emissions pathway.

The fuel cell approach would cut permitting time by 44 months—from 65.6 months down to 21.6—but still falls short of the 16-month target, and the EJ denial authority would still apply. I'm considering whether to search for alternate sites since the major nonattainment NSR trigger is clearly met, though the entire OTR region from Virginia northward operates under the 50 tpy statewide NOx rule, so relocating within 120 km likely won't escape that threshold. However, moving to Delaware or Maryland could sidestep the serious ozone nonattainment designation and New Jersey's EJ denial statute with its 1.6x multiplier, which would meaningfully change the regulatory pathway and agency requirements—worth exploring.

I've got 13 API calls remaining and plenty of credits, so I'll run the alternate site search with a smaller sample size and tighter radius to manage costs, then batch it with a retry of the class I area request using a specific location.

Combined cycle gets to 111 tpy but pulls the plant onto the List of 28 as a steam electric plant, dropping the PSD threshold to 100 tpy. Only the fuel cell flips the pathway to minor NSR.

The site fails on major nonattainment NSR, which is the condition for searching outward. Let me do that, and retry the Class I request with the example location it needs.

The field request failed again despite providing an example location—it seems to need a structured parameter that doesn't exist, which means Class I area distance is genuinely unobtainable due to a tool limitation. Looking at alternatives, the best option is New Castle, Delaware with about 42 months, still well short of the 16-month target and within the major NNSR constraint. Now I'm compiling the key findings: the origin site faces 66 months likely under major NNSR versus the 16-month target, while the best alternate still hits 42 months. A fuel cell at the current parcel drops to 21.6 months under minor NSR—the only real pathway shift—but still exceeds the target. Fuel cell at an alternate site in Delaware or Pennsylvania could potentially reach 12-14 months by clearing both EJ and state toxics, though that's speculative since I haven't tested it. However, there's a critical constraint: any gas-fired configuration, including fuel cells running on natural gas, triggers a 34 km lateral distance rule from Columbia Gas Trans, and the New Castle and Delaware County candidates have pipelines at 1.7 km and 0.9 km respectively. The site itself is essentially downtown Vineland with a school 343 meters away, a hospital at 178 meters, and 476 points of interest within 1 km—a densely populated urban area that compounds the EJ concerns.

## Closing assessment

**The pathway is major nonattainment NSR. Likely 66 months, range 41 to 104. The announced energization is 16 months away. This project does not switch on in 2027 as configured.**

**What decides it — three things.**

First, the county designation. Cumberland County is in **serious** nonattainment for the 2015 8-hour ozone NAAQS, Philadelphia-Atlantic City PA-NJ area (EPA Green Book, 40 CFR 81, fetched 2026-07-31). Serious classification sets the NOx major-source threshold at 50 tpy, not 250. New Jersey is also entirely inside the Ozone Transport Region under CAA 184, so that 50 tpy applies statewide regardless of what any local monitor says. There is no version of a 400 MW gas turbine that gets under 50 tpy NOx. Uncontrolled PTE is 5,887 tpy at 8760 hours. Synthetic minor is arithmetically real but commercially dead: it needs a 67 hr/yr cap, which is one percent availability. That is not a data center plant.

Second, the offsets. At 1.2:1 you must buy 7,064 tons of verified NOx reductions from existing sources inside the nonattainment area (CAA 173). LAER applies with no cost defense. This is the item I would underwrite first, because it is the one that can be simply unavailable at any price in a mature Northeast airshed.

Third, and this is the one that can kill it outright rather than delay it — **

steps.title: Switch to solid oxide fuel cells
steps.why: Solid oxide fuel cells emit almost no criteria pollutants, which usually takes the air permit off the critical path entirely. CO2 is not solved — they still burn gas. Much higher capital cost per MW, a supplier list you can count on one hand, and lead times that are themselves the constraint at data center scale.

options.cost_note: SCR is the standard NOx answer and it is also the expensive one: catalyst, reactor volume in the exhaust path, and an ammonia or urea storage and handling system on site, which brings its own safety review and often its own local permit. Small heat-rate penalty from the pressure drop. It does nothing for CO.

options.label: Add oxidation catalyst
options.config: 400 MW simple_cycle_turbine on natural_gas (oxidation_catalyst), no enforceable hour cap (PTE at 8760)
options.cost_note: An oxidation catalyst cuts CO by about 90% and VOC by about half. No reagent, no storage tank, small pressure drop, and it is cheap next to SCR. Worth checking first whenever CO is the pollutant sitting over the threshold — on an uncontrolled turbine that is more often the case than people expect.
